text: Morris Villarroel (born 1978 or 1979) is a Spanish professor of animal psychology at the Technical University of Madrid. Since February 2010, he has been lifelogging by writing in paper notebooks at 15 to 30 minute intervals, recording what he is doing, his location, the times he wakes up, the food he eats, and his ideas. He also tracks his movements using a fitness tracker. An example log entry reads: "I woke up at 05:45 in a hotel in Sweden. My hind leg muscles were hurting a bit." When notebooks are full, he indexes them in a spreadsheet with categories and keywords. In 2019, he estimated spending about an hour a day writing in his notebooks. Originally planning to continue for 10 years as an experiment, he decided to keep going after that period. He began lifelogging to improve his memory and time management and to maintain a clear record of his life experiences, which he says makes him feel like he has lived a longer life and enhances his emotional regulation. As of December 2019, he had filled up 307 notebooks. In April 2014, he started wearing a chest-mounted camera that took photos every 30 seconds, accumulating about 1,200 per day, which he used for most of the day except in private settings like the bedroom. He captured significant memories such as his father's death and his son's birth, and noted that while some people were uncomfortable, most were supportive. He discontinued using the camera after a few years due to difficulty managing the volume of photos. Both of his parents are psychologists, and he is married with five children.
